awd_titl_txt: Conference: Community Research Prioritization for Volcanoes Across the Alaska-Aleutian Arc Workshop
awd_abstract_narration:
Part 1: Volcanic eruptions create extreme and evolving hazards to nearby populations and commercial air traffic, with ~50-70 devastating events occurring worldwide each year. The Alaska-Aleutian arc, USA in particular poses high threats to a global aviation community due to its frequently active volcanoes (~2 eruptions and 6 unrest episodes per year) and its location beneath highly utilized North Pacific air routes. One avenue to strengthen the volcanology community’s ability to respond when unrest begins is to have a thorough understanding of the timescales of subsurface processes (e.g., magma movement) that have led to different size and styles of eruption (e.g., plume height). This progress can be accomplished through the integration of multiple datasets (petrology, gas geochemistry, seismology, geodesy) with near-real-time observations of volcanic unrest. Although significant advances have been made to understand the processes that fuel earthquakes and volcanic events in subduction zone centers over the past two decades, significant challenges remain with integrating different techniques for studying these systems (e.g., geophysics with petrology or gas emissions) as well as our ability to interpret the dense data streams collected during unrest events. To address these big picture needs, a three-day workshop will be held at the Alaska Volcano Observatory in Anchorage, Alaska, to highlight specifically chosen datasets and questions that require attention by the broader volcanology community. 

Part 2: Alaska is the most volcanically active region in the USA and one of the most active in the world. The high rate of volcanic activity, and along strike variations in subduction dynamics, provides an ideal laboratory to study the interplay between tectonic and volcanic processes. In May of 2025 a 3-day workshop will be hosted at the Alaska Volcano Observatory (AVO), a consortium of the USGS, University of Alaska Fairbanks, and State of Alaska Division of Geological & Geophysical Surveys, aimed at disseminating the current state of knowledge for potentially active volcanoes in Alaska and identifying compelling research directions. The high rates of volcanic activity in Alaska and the comprehensive data collected and archived by the Alaska Volcano Observatory make it the best place to study active volcanic processes at convergent-margin volcanoes in the United States. This is evidenced by several large-scale research efforts underway (PREEVENTS, AVERT) as well as proposed (CONVERSE, SZ4D) that see the benefit of studying the Alaska-Aleutian Arc. In addition, Alaska is home to other volcanoes, including recently restless Mount Edgecumbe and the massive and poorly understood Wrangell volcanic field. This as a crucial time for introducing interested scientists to the datasets and questions that are the highest priority for advancing the science pertaining to these active systems. By selecting datasets that answer crucial gaps in our knowledge, the community can tackle outstanding questions in this field and identify new mechanisms to advance our understanding of the drivers and timescales of processes within subduction zones that broadly fall into two fields: 1) improving our spatial reconstruction of the sub-surface systems that feed volcanic eruptions and 2) progress towards the interpretation and processing of datasets collected during volcanic unrest. Combining datasets allows for interdisciplinary, system-level questions to be asked and investigated, a crucial step to coordinating future efforts and resources, as well as centering science questions around solid, testable hypotheses.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
In May 2025, more than 70 scientists gathered in Anchorage, Alaska for the Alaska–Aleutian Arc Science Prioritization Workshop. The event brought together researchers at all career stages from universities, federal and state agencies, and research institutes across the United States. Their shared goal was to make better use of Alaska’s unparalleled volcano monitoring and geologic datasets to improve our understanding of how volcanoes work and how their hazards affect people.

Alaska is the most volcanically active region in the United States. Its volcanoes erupt frequently, threaten aviation routes critical to global commerce, and impact nearby communities and ecosystems. Fortunately, the Alaska Volcano Observatory (AVO) maintains one of the world’s most comprehensive volcano monitoring systems, collecting seismic, satellite, geodetic, gas, and geologic data. This workshop aimed to bring these data together with new ideas and new people to tackle fundamental science questions that also have real-world benefits.

Advancing Scientific Understanding (Intellectual Merit)

The workshop focused on two major scientific themes. First, participants worked to improve understanding of volcanic “plumbing systems”—the networks of magma storage and pathways beneath volcanoes that control when, where, and how eruptions occur. Second, they explored better ways to interpret the enormous volumes of data collected during volcanic unrest, when small changes can signal rising hazards.

A major outcome of the workshop was identifying priority volcanoes and datasets where interdisciplinary work can lead to breakthroughs. Scientists from different specialties (seismology, geodesy, geochemistry, petrology, remote sensing, and gas geochemistry) worked together to link subsurface processes with surface observations. For example, new collaborations formed around connecting volcanic gas emissions measured by satellites and aircraft with data collected from the erupted rocks. These efforts will help scientists interpret what gas signals observed during unrest mean about magma movement at depth.

Participants also identified key gaps in knowledge, such as limited isotopic data from eastern Alaska volcanoes and a need for better chronologies of past eruptions. Addressing these gaps will allow researchers to compare volcanic systems across the arc and understand why some volcanoes produce large, explosive eruptions while others erupt frequently but gently. By prioritizing shared datasets and coordinated studies, the workshop laid the groundwork for community-driven science that moves beyond isolated case studies to system-level understanding.

Several focused working groups emerged from the workshop and remain active. These groups are developing integrated databases, preparing collaborative conference presentations, and drafting future research proposals. Early progress includes coordinated analyses of historical eruptions, new frameworks for categorizing volcanic earthquakes, and pilot studies that combine geophysical imaging with petrologic evidence of magma storage and ascent. Three AGU abstracts were submitted, and a follow up workshop occurred at AGU in December of 2025. In addition several papers and grant proposals are currently under development.

Benefits for Society (Broader Impacts)

The broader impacts of this effort extend well beyond academic science. Improving understanding of volcanic processes directly supports hazard assessment and eruption forecasting in Alaska. Better interpretation of seismic and satellite signals can provide earlier warning of eruptions, reducing risks to aviation, infrastructure, and nearby communities. 

The workshop also emphasized open science and equitable access. Participants were trained in how to find and use publicly available AVO datasets and geologic samples, lowering barriers for researchers new to Alaska or from smaller institutions. Samples housed at the Geologic Materials Center (Anchorage) and data archived in open repositories ensure that future studies can build on this work without duplicating effort; a group tour to this facility highlighted how the respository worked, with several researchers taking samples for new projects. 

An important outcome was community building. Early‑career scientists participated alongside senior researchers and observatory staff, forming mentorship and collaboration networks that will shape volcano science for years to come. The workshop actively worked to broaden participation by welcoming researchers from diverse skillsets and institutions and by creating shared spaces for continued engagement.

Public outreach was also a priority. An episode of AVO Radio aired across Alaska during the workshop, translating the science for local communities and highlighting why volcano research matters for everyday life in the state. Recorded talks and resources were made publicly available online, extending the workshop’s reach beyond those who could attend in person.

Taken together, the Alaska–Aleutian Arc Science Prioritization Workshop strengthened the scientific foundation for understanding one of Earth’s most dynamic volcanic regions. It advanced fundamental knowledge of how magma is generated, stored, and erupts, while directly supporting hazard mitigation and public safety. Perhaps most importantly, it demonstrated how collaborative, open, and interdisciplinary science can turn rich data into knowledge that benefits both science and society.
